Australia's first government look at AI and jobs found that the sky is not falling. Between November 2022 and February 2026, employment in the fifth of occupations most exposed to AI grew 5.6 per cent, against 9.5 per cent in the least exposed fifth, unemployment sat at 4.2 per cent, and young graduates are still finding work. That reads as reassurance, and I think it is a reason for care rather than comfort.

A blue-collar worker usually gets to watch disruption arrive. A plant has a closure date and a contract has an end, so even a bad notice gives a person something to act on. White-collar disruption is unlikely to come with a notice. It shows up as a requisition that never opens, a graduate intake trimmed by a few places, or a team that stays the same size while the work grows. Nobody is dismissed, so nothing appears in the layoff headlines, and the aggregate data moves very little. The department's own model puts employment in exposed occupations about 2 per cent below the pre-ChatGPT trend, and it warns that the estimate is sensitive to modelling choices. Indeed found graduate postings fell almost 15 per cent last year, and judged the timing too early to blame AI. Those are honest caveats, and they also show how hard this is to see in the numbers while it is happening.

My view is that the first signal will be a pipeline thinning quietly. The tasks that used to teach people their trade, the first draft, the reconciliation, the first pass at the contract, are the ones most easily handed to software, and the gain is booked straight away while the cost arrives years later as a shortage of people who have learned to exercise judgement.

Two questions for any leadership team. Which roles in your organisation have stopped being backfilled in the past year, and was that a decision or a drift? And where will your next generation of senior people learn the work you are automating today?

#FutureOfWork #AustralianBusiness #Workforce

What I've done this year
It's been one year since I graduated with my degree in Computer Science. Here's what I've been working on since.
Reps
Reps is my work-in-progress personal training app, built around three years of training clients and writing their programs. So far it has a full database schema (pictured is a sample), an API contract, a basic MCP server, and a React + TypeScript frontend. Planned features include trainer and client accounts, program editing, messaging, calendar-synced scheduling, session packages, and an AI virtual trainer. Next up: finishing the backend, containerizing with Docker, and launching on the web, with Android and iOS to follow.
workout-xlsx2html
The mini project that kicked off Reps. My training programs lived in spreadsheets, which are really just data. I wrote a Python tool that reads them with openpyxl into custom dataclass structures designed for transferability and interoperability. That data modeling became the foundation for the Reps schema.
Self-Hosted Cloud Infrastructure
My self-hosted cloud keeps getting upgrades for performance, security, and reliability. It runs on Gentoo Linux with Docker Compose, PostgreSQL, Redis, and QEMU VMs. This year I completed a major Gentoo profile upgrade and used it to harden the system with SELinux, Secure Boot, and full disk encryption. I also added Grafana for monitoring, Ollama for local LLMs, and Woodpecker for CI.
Anthropic Academy
My degree gave me a strong AI/ML foundation, but keeping current is an ongoing effort. I've been working through Anthropic Academy, including Introduction to Model Context Protocol, Claude Code 101, and Claude Code in Action. I learn best by building, so I put the MCP material straight to work in the Reps MCP server.
Reading

- The Biostar Handbook is really a masterclass in command-line data processing and reproducible pipelines. I read it out of curiosity about where software meets biology and health.

Malaysia has secured RM385.7 billion in Data Center investments since 2021. But let’s look at the actual math behind the workforce.

We celebrate the mega-campuses rising in Johor and Cyberjaya, funded by hyperscalers like AWS, Oracle, ByteDance, and Microsoft. But how much of this capital is actually translating into jobs for everyday Malaysians?

Let’s break down the reality of the numbers:
💰 The Investment vs. Direct Jobs: A standard 50MW AI-ready data center costs roughly RM 2 Billion to build. Once operational, it only requires 30 to 50 direct specialists (Critical Facility Engineers, Site Operations). The direct labor density is incredibly low, though the pay is highly lucrative (often RM 10,000 - RM 15,000+ for senior roles).

📈 The Estimated Benefit (The Potential): Macro models show a 4.2x multiplier for data centers. For every direct job, over 3 indirect jobs are supposed to be created in specialized MEP construction, fiber optics, and physical security. By 2030, this sector is projected to support 130,000 to 190,000 jobs across the ecosystem.

🛑 The Actual Translation (The Reality): Despite the massive projections, a significant chunk of these roles is bypassing the local workforce entirely:

The Baseline Trades: For structured cabling, rack assembly, and site preparation, Tier-1 contractors compress sub-contractor margins so tightly that they default to foreign contract labor. Thousands of capable local SPM and diploma leavers are left underemployed in the gig economy (p-hailing) because local wages are artificially depressed by this cost-arbitrage.

The Management Tier: To manage the risk of billion-ringgit assets, hyperscalers frequently parachute in expatriate directors from regional hubs rather than promoting locally, while our top-tier local cloud architects get poached across the Causeway to Singapore.

The Hard Truth: Malaysia does not lack talent. We lack a system that forces the translation of CapEx into local jobs. We are at risk of building high-tech economic enclaves where 70% of the CapEx goes to imported hardware, baseline construction goes to foreign quotas, and the local grid bears the water and power strain.

To fix this, we need strict Local-First Prioritization Gates before any foreign worker quotas are approved for sub-contractors, and we need direct SPM-to-Tech apprenticeships to pull local youth straight onto the data hall floor.

I want to open this up to the HR leaders, tech operators, and EPC contractors in my network:How do we enforce local-first hiring and bridge this talent gap without slowing down the aggressive 18-month construction deadlines developers are facing?

I won’t share the details because they involve confidential business information and trade secrets.

✅ Approximately 20 hours of work saved per month across the activities we targeted.
✅ Improvements to recruitment workflows, including reducing delays in the hiring process.
✅ Opportunities to streamline interview coordination, approval workflows and decision-making processes.

Was 20 hours a month a massive transformation? No, and I wouldn’t claim that it was. It was an initial pilot, not a completed, enterprise-wide transformation.

For me, this is what AI transformation should look like. Understand the business first. Identify the real problems. Implement thoughtfully. Measure the results. Then build on what works.

I’m not interested in implementing AI just to say a company is using AI. I’m interested in making it work for the business and the people behind it.

That’s where the real value begins.

What happens when a product quietly destroys its own suppliers?

An internal Microsoft document already answered that question.

"Our AI content strategy has started a 'doom loop' that will hurt the performance of our models and the entire web at the same time."

That line surfaced in unredacted filings in the New York Times lawsuit against Microsoft and OpenAI. Another passage: "It is highly unusual that an end-product threatens the economic foundations of its essential suppliers."

Read that as a risk officer, not a journalist.

The loop is simple. AI answers the question, so nobody visits the source. The source loses revenue and stops producing. The model now learns from less, and from more of its own output.

The same pattern is already running inside companies.

Greenhouse CEO Daniel Chait put it this way about hiring: "more AI use begets more AI use, to no one's benefit." Candidates generate résumés. Recruiters screen them with AI. Nobody learns anything.

Your knowledge base can do the same thing. AI drafts the policy. AI summarizes the policy. Next year, AI drafts from the summary.

Three controls I'd put in place:

1. Label provenance. Know which internal documents a person wrote or approved.

2. Protect your sources of truth. Policies, procedures, and contracts need a named human owner, not just a generator.

3. Measure the loop. Track where AI output becomes AI input, and audit quality at that point.

AI that feeds on its own output does not get smarter. It gets more confident.

Where in your organization is AI already reading what AI wrote?

I lined up competitor pitch decks. Same logos, different story. If companies say, offer & price the same way, customers have one tool left: price. M. Porter made this point in 1996. Doing the same activities better than rivals is operational effectiveness. Strategy is choosing to be different and deciding what you will not do.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝗮 𝗼𝗳 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹
Look at staffing in India. ISF data shows overall staffing grew 5.8% year on year in Q2FY26, and IT staffing grew 16%. ISF notes gross margins for contract staffing firms sit between 2% and 8%, with net margins well below that. Thats what a market looks like when too many players sell the same thing. Salesforce found 73% of customers expect better personalisation as technology evolves, yet 61% say most companies treat them as a number. That gap is an open door.

𝗦𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗸
𝟭. 𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 is something the customer can feel, not just claim.
𝟮. 𝗖𝗼𝘀𝘁:Being the low-cost player is a valid strategy. Drifting into low prices because you have little else to offer is not. The first is built into operations. The second erodes margin.
𝟯. 𝗦𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: A recruiter who understands cybersecurity hiring, or a media team that knows B2B tech, gets called first and negotiated with less. Narrowing your focus often widens your margin.
𝟰. 𝗖𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗰𝘆: Know a clients hiring calendar, approval politics and what went wrong with their vendor, and you stop being a supplier and become hard to replace. Yet 55% feel theyre dealing with separate departments rather than one company. That needs fixing.
𝟱. 𝗦𝗽𝗲𝗲𝗱 isnt just client turnaround. Its how fast you decide. McKinsey found only 20% of executives say their organisations excel at decision making. Those that decide fast and execute quickly see better returns.
𝟲. 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆: If everyone buys the same tools, technology becomes table stakes, not an edge. The advantage is in how you use it. Companies getting real value from AI achieve 1.7x revenue growth and 1.6x EBIT margin compared with laggards. Same technology, different results.
𝟳. 𝗚𝗲𝗼𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗵𝘆: Sometimes the edge is where you play. Indias GCCs employed 2.36 million people in FY26, mostly crowded into a few metros. Yet tier-2 and tier-3 cities already hosted over 220 GCCs by 2024. Whoever builds talent pipelines in Coimbatore, Nashik or Kochi early will have an advantage.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗜 𝗸𝗲𝗲𝗽 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝘁𝗼
Pick one or two, go deep, and say no to business that pulls you away. Ask leadership teams: if your three biggest competitors disappeared tomorrow, would customers notice anything missing? Or would they move to the next vendor with the same deck? If its the 2nd, you have a business plan. Not yet a strategy.

The duty of care belongs to whoever holds the kill switch
Texas has opened public consultation on administrative enforcement rules under HB 1709, setting the compliance architecture for high-risk algorithmic systems. The draft rules detail deployer risk assessments, mandatory discrimination disclosures, and an explicit duty to suspend non-compliant systems within ten days of discovering a risk.
The bill is being reported as an algorithmic bias statute; it is actually a statutory duty of care imposed directly on enterprise deployers. The law distinguishes between the developer who builds the model and the deployer who runs it, assigning independent liability to the latter. You cannot contract out of that duty by pointing to the software licence.
The obvious objection is that deployers cannot verify the mathematical neutrality of an outsourced black box. That is true, and the statute answers it flatly; where a deployer has reason to believe a system causes algorithmic discrimination, its sole statutory defence is immediate suspension. A process that documents bias without pausing the deployment is not compliance; it is an admission.
For in-house teams deploying AI in hiring, customer evaluation, or automated underwriting, this changes the operational playbook. Draft an algorithmic suspension protocol alongside your disaster recovery plan, because legal exposure accrues daily while a flawed model remains live. Verify that your commercial agreements require vendors to deliver impact assessment data on demand, rather than under non-disclosure caveats.
Regulation that demands continuous review does not create safety; it creates an operational duty to pull the plug.

She took a chance and pitched him to her CEO. He took one look at the portfolio and said, “If you like him, hire him.”

She did, and he performed far beyond expectations. Before long, he was running an entire major workstream for the company, handling everything from purchasing heavy industrial equipment to negotiating complex legal contracts. He did not succeed because he knew how to do all of that on day one. He succeeded because whenever he hit a wall, he figured out a way through it.

“If we had used automated AI screening back then, we would have missed him entirely.”

Her story hit home because I know exactly what it feels like to be rejected before anyone gives you time to explain what you can actually do.

Back when I was looking to pivot into the private sector, headhunters repeatedly contacted me about Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) manager roles, the exact work I was already doing. But whenever I applied for Government Affairs, Public Policy, Strategic Communications, or Corporate Liaison roles, I hit a brick wall. I was invisible because automated keyword filters instantly dropped my CV for lacking specific corporate job titles.

I used to find this infuriating. Over time, I realized it stemmed from a structural problem in talent acquisition. Human recruiters act as intermediaries. Unlike hiring managers, who understand their teams’ needs and can take a calculated gamble on raw talent, recruiters rarely have the safety net or domain authority to deviate from the script. They stick closely to the job description because that is how their performance is measured.

When AI hiring platforms first came along, I wrote them off instantly. I assumed they simply digitized our worst screening habits. My recruiter friend smirked and agreed: “Candidates don’t want to be interviewed by an algorithm anyway.”

But it turns out we were both wrong. Looking at what this new wave of HR technology can actually do, I actually hope that more recruiters will use AI, with outsized benefits for career pivoters.

A business owner once told me their biggest fear wasn't bad marketing — it was being ghosted by the senior team the moment the contract was signed.

That fear isn't unfounded. It happens more than it should.

So here are 5 honest answers to the questions business owners are often too polite to ask before hiring an agency:

1. Will I get handed off to someone junior? Not with us. The experienced people in your pitch are the same ones doing the work.

2. Is AI doing all the work now? We use AI as a tool, not a replacement. Strategy, creativity and understanding what makes your business unique still need human judgement.

3. Is my work outsourced to the cheapest option? No. The people executing your strategy actually understand it — and you.

4. Am I just another account? Your business matters enormously to you, so it needs to matter to us too. We care about real outcomes, not vanity activity.

5. Will I end up managing the agency? You know your business. We know marketing. You shouldn't have to chase updates or become a marketing expert to get results.

The best agency relationships are built on trust, transparency and genuinely understanding the business behind the brand.

If you're evaluating a new agency, these are the questions worth asking.

Google: The Human Cost 

We talk endlessly about traffic drops, algorithm updates, and SEO volatility. We look at charts, traffic trending down and huge revenue falls. But we rarely talk about the human beings behind those all this. 

Over the last few months Google has doubled down and doubled down again in a quest that will result in the destruction of most of the Open Web. Thousands of independent publishers, journalists, and small businesses have seen their lives and livelihoods completely torn apart. People who spent a decade or more building honest businesses, hiring family, friends and colleagues who became close, and pouring their savings and energy into creating valuable content woke up to find their traffic has been syphoned off by a monopolist.

But this isn't just an economic shift - it's a mental health and emotional trauma for the individuals Google has callously impacted. The psychological toll of watching your livelihood vanish - not because your product wasn't good enough or because users didn't value your content - but because a trillion-dollar monopoly started tweaking lines of code. All this breeds a profound sense of anxiety, powerlessness, and despair. Behind every failing website is a family trying to figure out how to pay a mortgage, and an entrepreneur facing the devastating reality that their hard work was used against them, without permission or payment, to feed an AI answer engine all in the name of greed and supposed 'progress'. 

The unwritten social contract of the internet was clear: give Google your data, and Google will give you an audience. If Google intended to abandon that implied contract, strip-mine our data, and trap our users on its own platforms, it surely had a profound moral responsibility to be transparent and upfront about it way ahead of time. It had a duty to be open, honest, and clear about its ultimate intentions. Instead, creators were kept in the dark, constantly told to keep creating high-quality content (abiding by Google's ever-changing guidance), while the ground was quickly cut out from beneath them without warning, or a care for the consequences.

Innovation should never require the systematic, ruthless destruction by Google of the people who helped build it's platform. To the thousands of creators out there feeling the crushing weight of this shift: you are not a failure, and you are not alone. Your work had value - it was Google who decided to dictate how quality was defined and chose to deplatform you because it suited its business model to do so. It's the monopolist who now decides who sees what on the internet - controlling and manipulating data for its own commercial gain. It's surely time to finally hold Google accountable not just for its market monopoly, but for the human lives disrupted purely for corporate greed. Lawmakers and regulators need to act now to stop Google's unethical, heartless and callous behaviour - before the human costs become too much for many to bear.

One thing contract AI work teaches you very quickly:

One contract is not a career plan.

I’m currently working across multiple AI-training and evaluation contracts, and they all behave differently.

One has active work but a weekly hour cap.

One has been on hold for nearly three months, even though the team lead is still trying to get it restarted.

Another is temporarily paused while the client restructures.

Another provides steady work, but only for a limited number of hours each day.

Then there are the applications, interviews, “selected” statuses, and hiring-manager reviews that may or may not turn into actual production work.

At some point, it stops feeling like having “a job.”

It starts feeling like managing a small portfolio.

The technical work can be completely different too.

One project may involve evaluating AI-generated professional artifacts.

Another may involve robot-video annotation, action segmentation, retries, object-state tracking, and QA of AI-generated captions.

The common thread is quality control:

Understand the instructions.
Inspect the evidence.
Identify the failure mode.
Document the result clearly.

But the skill nobody really puts in the job description is pipeline management.

A good project can stop for reasons that have nothing to do with your performance.

Clients restructure.
Batches disappear.
Budgets pause.
A team may still want the project to continue while everyone waits for approval upstream.

So you keep multiple lanes open.

A good contract pays you.

A good portfolio keeps you working.

Customer service representative, tier 1.
🎧 Salesforce cut about 4,000 support roles after ticket volume fell. In announcements that name AI, customer support is the most-replaced job — roughly 71,500 seats at 14 companies since 2024. The seat that goes is the rep on password resets, order status, and refund policy. The rep on a cancellation threat stays. The Bureau of Labor Statistics has customer service representatives on a −5.5% path through 2034, off a base of 2.8 million.

Data entry keyer. ⌨️ 
About 142,000 people in the U.S. still hold this title, median pay around $43,000. The BLS outlook is −26% by 2034, the steepest on the clerical list. Keying invoices, applications, and form fields into a database is a solved task. The title does not get a successor. It gets absorbed by the system that used to receive the file.

Telemarketer. 
📞 About 67,000 telemarketers, outlook −22% through 2034. A voice tool can hold the script, the lead list, and the disposition code. An account executive is a different job. A dialer reading a fixed pitch is not.

Bookkeeping clerk, payroll clerk, and executive secretary. 
📒 The World Economic Forum puts data-entry clerks, executive secretaries, and accounting, bookkeeping, and payroll clerks at more than half of the job destruction employers expect, with 25–35% less demand for those seats. 

Legal secretary and junior paralegal on first-pass review. 
📄 Scan, extract, compare, flag. A 2026 ranking of 756 jobs put telephone operators at 83% exposure and legal secretaries and administrative assistants at 64%. Contract translators on standard commercial text are already in a draft-and-check workflow. Court interpreters and litigators are not.

Junior copywriter and production graphic designer. 
✍️ Product blurbs, ad variants, and first-pass layout. One 2026 tracker put junior copywriter hiring down about 25% and entry graphic design down about 19%. The campaign lead stays.
